title: Renal Weeks 1–4: physiology, disease, voiding and tumours — 18 questions

steps.title: Renal Weeks 1–4: from blood flow to urinary findings
steps.body:
Eighteen single-best-answer questions for Year 2 revision.

Week 1: renal perfusion, urine concentration and sodium–water balance.
Week 2: acute kidney injury and glomerular syndromes.
Week 3: normal voiding and renal tumours.
Week 4: haematuria and proteinuria.

Choose one answer, explain the mechanism, then discuss the revealed explanation. Allow about 65–80 minutes, or split the lesson into two sessions.

Q1–Q10 cover the four-week overview. Q11–Q13 extend sodium balance and blood-pressure physiology; Q14–Q18 extend glomerulonephritis.

steps.prompt: A patient with severe bilateral renal artery stenosis develops a marked fall in GFR soon after starting an ACE inhibitor. Which change most directly explains the fall in filtration?

options.text: Afferent arteriolar constriction raises glomerular capillary pressure.
Efferent arteriolar constriction lowers glomerular capillary pressure.
Reduced angiotensin II causes efferent arteriolar dilation and lowers glomerular capillary pressure.
Increased collecting-duct water permeability directly lowers glomerular capillary pressure.

steps.explanation: C. With reduced renal perfusion, angiotensin II helps support glomerular pressure through efferent arteriolar constriction. ACE inhibition removes this support, so GFR can fall markedly when both kidneys depend on it. This haemodynamic effect does not mean ACE inhibitors are generally harmful to kidneys. Source: renal autoregulation review; KDIGO AKI guidance.

steps.title: Follow the blood, then locate the resistance
steps.body:
Renal artery → segmental → interlobar → arcuate → cortical radiate arteries → afferent arteriole → glomerular capillaries → efferent arteriole → peritubular capillaries or vasa recta → veins.

Myogenic and macula-densa feedback mainly adjust afferent resistance to stabilise flow and filtration over a limited pressure range. Severe hypovolaemia and sympathetic activation reduce renal blood flow; autoregulation cannot fully compensate.

Angiotensin II can support filtration pressure during low perfusion, but severe vasoconstriction may reduce both flow and GFR.

steps.title: How Medicines Change Glomerular Pressure

steps.prompt: A dehydrated patient has high circulating vasopressin but receives a loop diuretic that blocks NKCC2 in the thick ascending limb. Why does this reduce the maximum concentration the kidney can achieve?

options.text: The thick ascending limb becomes freely permeable to water.
Reduced NaCl transport into the medulla weakens the osmotic gradient needed for collecting-duct water reabsorption.
Vasopressin can no longer bind to V2 receptors anywhere in the kidney.
Urea is no longer filtered at the glomerulus.

steps.explanation: B. The water-impermeable thick ascending limb reabsorbs NaCl, helping build the corticomedullary gradient. Blocking NKCC2 weakens that gradient. Even when vasopressin makes the collecting duct water-permeable, less osmotic driving force remains for water recovery. V2 receptors and urea filtration are not abolished. Sources: urinary concentration and medullary architecture reviews.

steps.title: A gradient plus a water-permeable exit
steps.body:
The loop system helps establish a medullary osmotic gradient; urea recycling contributes, especially in the inner medulla.

Vasa recta countercurrent exchange helps preserve the gradient.

Vasopressin acts at V2 receptors, promoting apical aquaporin-2 insertion in collecting-duct principal cells. Water then moves down an osmotic gradient.

A concentrating defect can arise from failure of either the gradient or the water-permeability response.

steps.prompt: A healthy adult drinks a large water load. Plasma osmolality falls slightly. Which renal response best limits dilution of plasma sodium?

options.text: Reduced vasopressin release, lower collecting-duct water permeability and excretion of dilute urine
Increased vasopressin release, greater collecting-duct water permeability and retention of free water
Increased aldosterone secretion to directly detect and correct the low plasma sodium concentration
Increased proximal NaCl loss without any change in water handling

steps.explanation: A. Lower osmolality suppresses vasopressin, reducing collecting-duct water permeability and allowing excretion of excess water. Plasma sodium reflects water relative to exchangeable sodium and potassium; it is not a direct measure of total-body sodium stores. Aldosterone mainly regulates sodium retention and extracellular volume, rather than directly sensing plasma sodium concentration. Sources: water-homeostasis and sodium-balance physiology reviews.

steps.title: Separate concentration from content
steps.body:
Plasma sodium concentration: strongly influenced by water balance, with thirst and vasopressin adjusting intake and renal water excretion.

Total-body sodium: strongly influences extracellular fluid volume. Renal Na+ excretion is adjusted through the renin–angiotensin–aldosterone system, sympathetic activity, natriuretic signals and pressure natriuresis.

Volume depletion can stimulate vasopressin despite low osmolality. Ask separately: what is the sodium concentration, and what is the effective circulating volume?

steps.prompt:
Three patients develop acute kidney injury.
1: Severe diarrhoea, hypotension and improvement in renal function after restoration of perfusion.
2: Prolonged shock followed by persistent renal dysfunction and muddy-brown granular casts.
3: Acute urinary retention with bilateral hydronephrosis.

Which sequence best identifies their principal mechanisms?

options.text: 1: tubular epithelial injury; 2: urinary obstruction; 3: reduced renal perfusion
1: urinary obstruction; 2: reduced renal perfusion; 3: tubular epithelial injury
1: reduced renal perfusion; 2: urinary obstruction; 3: immune-mediated glomerular injury
1: reduced renal perfusion; 2: acute tubular injury; 3: urinary obstruction

steps.explanation: D. Case 1 is prerenal hypoperfusion; case 2 suggests intrinsic acute tubular injury after sustained ischaemia; case 3 is postrenal obstruction. Persistent hypoperfusion can progress to structural injury. Sepsis-associated AKI is multifactorial, so not every case is explained by low blood pressure alone. Evaluate reversible causes promptly. Source: KDIGO AKI guidance.

steps.title: AKI: use the mechanism to organise the differential
steps.body:
Prerenal: reduced effective renal perfusion, for example volume depletion, haemorrhage or low-output heart failure.

Intrinsic: tubular injury from ischaemia or toxins; interstitial nephritis; glomerulonephritis; vascular disease.

Postrenal: obstruction, for example retention, bilateral ureteric obstruction or obstruction of a solitary functioning kidney.

AKI criteria include creatinine rise ≥26.5 µmol/L within 48 hours, ≥1.5 times baseline within 7 days, or urine output <0.5 mL/kg/hour for at least 6 hours. A normal urine volume does not exclude AKI.

steps.prompt: Patient A has cola-coloured urine, hypertension, reduced GFR, red-cell casts and urine protein of 1 g/day. Patient B has generalised oedema, urine protein of 5.2 g/day, serum albumin of 20 g/L and hyperlipidaemia, without red-cell casts. Which pairing best identifies the dominant syndromes and mechanisms?

options.text: A: nephrotic syndrome from increased glomerular protein permeability; B: nephritic syndrome from glomerular inflammation
A: nephritic syndrome from glomerular inflammation; B: nephrotic syndrome from increased glomerular protein permeability
A: tubular proteinuria from impaired protein reabsorption; B: overflow proteinuria from excess protein production
A: postrenal impairment from urinary obstruction; B: nephrotic syndrome from increased glomerular protein permeability

steps.explanation: B. A has a nephritic pattern: haematuria with active sediment, impaired filtration and often hypertension. B has nephrotic-range protein loss with hypoalbuminaemia and oedema; adult nephrotic-range proteinuria is conventionally >3.5 g/day. Nephritic and nephrotic features may overlap. Neither syndrome alone establishes the precise histological diagnosis. Sources: KDIGO glomerular disease guidance; NIDDK.

steps.title: Name the syndrome before naming the disease
steps.body:
Nephritic patterns: IgA nephropathy, infection-related GN, lupus nephritis and rapidly progressive forms such as ANCA-associated or anti-GBM disease.

Nephrotic patterns: minimal change disease, FSGS, membranous nephropathy and diabetic kidney disease.

Glomerulonephritis denotes inflammatory glomerular injury; not every glomerular disease is inflammatory.

Urine sediment, renal function, clinical context and targeted serology help refine the cause. Biopsy is used when indicated, rather than diagnosing a specific lesion from protein quantity alone.

steps.prompt: An adult with intact neurological pathways decides to void. Which coordinated change best describes normal micturition?

options.text: Increased hypogastric sympathetic activity relaxes the detrusor and contracts the outlet.
Increased pudendal activity contracts the external sphincter while the detrusor contracts.
Pontine coordination increases sacral pelvic parasympathetic activity and reduces pudendal sphincter activity, allowing detrusor contraction with outlet relaxation.
The external sphincter opens only when abdominal pressure exceeds a persistently contracted outlet.

steps.explanation: C. Bladder afferent signalling is integrated with higher control through brainstem circuits. During voiding, pelvic parasympathetic output from S2–S4 promotes detrusor contraction, while reduced somatic pudendal drive relaxes the external urethral sphincter and the outlet relaxes. Storage instead favours a relaxed, compliant bladder and a closed outlet. Sources: neural-control-of-micturition reviews.

steps.title: Storage and voiding are coordinated states
steps.body:
Storage: low-pressure filling; sympathetic signalling supports detrusor relaxation and outlet resistance. Pudendal somatic activity maintains external sphincter tone.

Voiding: bladder stretch input and cortical permission engage pontine coordination. Pelvic parasympathetic activity rises; sympathetic and external-sphincter somatic activity falls.

Detrusor pressure must exceed outlet pressure for flow. A weak detrusor or a non-relaxing outlet can impair emptying despite an urge to void.

steps.prompt: A fit 60-year-old has painless visible haematuria. Multiphasic CT shows a 3.2-cm enhancing solid renal cortical mass confined to the kidney, without venous invasion or metastases. The anatomy permits nephron-sparing surgery. After specialist assessment and shared decision-making, intervention is chosen for suspected localised RCC. Which treatment generally offers cancer control while preserving renal tissue?

options.text: Immediate systemic immunotherapy as the standard treatment for any enhancing mass
Partial nephrectomy when technically and oncologically feasible
Mandatory radical nephrectomy with routine removal of a normal ipsilateral adrenal gland
Radiotherapy alone as the routine first choice for a fit surgical candidate

steps.explanation: B. Partial nephrectomy is generally recommended for feasible T1 tumours and preserves more functioning renal tissue. An enhancing mass is suspicious but imaging does not prove its histology. Biopsy, surveillance, ablation or other approaches depend on the clinical setting and preferences. Radical nephrectomy and adrenal removal are not automatic for every small renal mass. Sources: EAU RCC diagnostic and management guidance.

steps.title: An enhancing renal mass starts an assessment
steps.body:
RCC may be incidental or present with haematuria; the full classic triad is not required.

Contrast-enhanced cross-sectional imaging characterises the mass and assesses extent. Biopsy is considered when it will inform management, and is needed before some non-surgical treatments.

For suitable localised tumours, preserve nephrons where possible. Larger, complex or advanced lesions require a different plan.

Management is based on anatomy, renal function, fitness, staging and patient preference.

steps.prompt: A renal cortical tumour contains clear cells in a rich capillary network and has loss of VHL function. Imaging also shows extension into the renal vein, but no distant metastases. Which statement best links its biology to its staging implications?

options.text: This is a benign oncocytoma; venous invasion has no staging significance.
VHL loss suppresses hypoxia-inducible signalling, and renal-vein invasion proves distant metastatic disease.
A tumour is always T1 when its diameter is below 7 cm, even if it invades the renal vein.
The findings support clear-cell RCC; VHL loss promotes hypoxia-inducible signalling, and renal-vein invasion places it in a locally advanced T category.

steps.explanation: D. Loss of VHL function promotes HIF-dependent signalling, including angiogenic pathways, characteristic of clear-cell RCC. Renal-vein or segmental-branch invasion is T3a; small size does not preserve a T1 classification when this invasion is present. Venous invasion is not itself distant metastasis and does not automatically preclude surgery. Stage, grade and spread help determine prognosis. Sources: EAU RCC pathology and staging guidance.

steps.title: Tumour type and extent answer different questions
steps.body:
RCC: clear-cell is the commonest subtype; papillary and chromophobe RCC are other important types. Extent and grade influence prognosis.

Oncocytoma: a benign epithelial tumour that can resemble RCC on imaging; a central scar does not establish benignity.

Classic angiomyolipoma: contains vessels, smooth muscle and fat. Haemorrhage risk influences management. Fat-poor lesions can be diagnostically difficult.

Wilms tumour is an important childhood renal malignancy, with a different diagnostic and treatment pathway.

Do not call every renal mass RCC, or every small mass harmless.

steps.prompt: Patient A has dysmorphic urinary red cells, red-cell casts and albuminuria. Patient B, an older smoker, has painless visible haematuria with clots and predominantly uniform red cells. Which interpretation is most appropriate?

options.text: A strongly suggests a glomerular source; B suggests a non-glomerular source and needs urological assessment.
A proves bladder cancer; B proves IgA nephropathy.
Both must originate in the glomeruli because all urinary red cells have passed through a kidney.
B can be observed without assessment because clots exclude malignancy.

steps.explanation: A. Dysmorphic cells, especially acanthocytes, and red-cell casts strongly support renal parenchymal, usually glomerular, bleeding. Clots favour non-glomerular bleeding, but cannot identify its exact site. Painless visible haematuria in an older smoker requires assessment for urinary tract malignancy. Morphology alone is imperfect, and suspected glomerular disease does not remove a separate indication for urological evaluation. Sources: AUA haematuria curriculum and guidance.

steps.title: Confirm blood cells, then consider the source
steps.body:
A positive dipstick for blood can reflect red cells, haemoglobin or myoglobin; microscopy helps distinguish them.

Glomerular clues: dysmorphic red cells, red-cell casts, albuminuria and impaired filtration.

Non-glomerular causes include stones, infection, prostatic disease, trauma and urinary tract tumours. Menstrual contamination can mimic haematuria.

Do not rely on urine colour, pain or red-cell shape alone. Persistent or visible haematuria needs assessment appropriate to the clinical context.

steps.prompt:
Three patients have proteinuria.
1: Long-standing diabetes with predominantly urinary albumin.
2: Proximal tubular injury with increased urinary low-molecular-weight proteins.
3: A plasma-cell disorder producing excessive filtered free light chains.

Which sequence best describes their predominant proteinuria mechanisms?

options.text: 1: overflow; 2: glomerular; 3: tubular
1: tubular; 2: overflow; 3: glomerular
1: glomerular leakage; 2: impaired tubular reabsorption; 3: overflow
1: lower urinary tract bleeding; 2: normal ageing; 3: exercise-related albuminuria

steps.explanation: C. Glomerular barrier abnormalities increase albumin leakage. Proximal tubular dysfunction reduces recovery of normally filtered low-molecular-weight proteins. Excess light-chain production causes overflow proteinuria, and may also injure tubules. An albumin-focused dipstick can miss non-albumin proteins. Quantify and investigate the pattern rather than treating all proteinuria as equivalent. Sources: KDIGO CKD guidance; NCI plasma-cell neoplasms PDQ.

steps.title: Confirm persistence and identify the protein
steps.body:
Common persistent causes include diabetic kidney disease and other glomerular disorders. Tubular disease and excess light-chain production produce different patterns.

Exercise, fever and infection can cause transient increases; orthostatic proteinuria is another consideration, especially in younger people.

A first-morning urine ACR is useful for albumin assessment; PCR and targeted protein studies may add information when non-albumin protein is suspected. Repeat testing and interpret alongside sediment, blood pressure and renal function.

steps.prompt: A 38-year-old woman with nephrotic syndrome presents with worsening leg swelling and abdominal distension. She has gained 6 kg over two weeks. Plasma sodium is 126 mmol/L, measured plasma osmolality is 264 mOsm/kg and blood glucose is normal. She has not taken diuretics and has had no vomiting or diarrhoea. Which pattern of total-body sodium and water best accounts for these findings?

options.text: Reduced total-body sodium and water, with a proportionately greater reduction in sodium.
Increased total-body sodium and water, with a proportionately greater increase in water.
Increased total-body sodium and water, with a proportionately greater increase in sodium.
Increased total-body sodium and water, with the sodium-to-water relationship preserved.

steps.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Increased total-body sodium and water, with a proportionately greater increase in water.

Why it is correct: Weight gain and worsening oedema in this patient favour sodium and water retention. Low measured osmolality confirms hypotonic hyponatraemia. Water has increased disproportionately to exchangeable sodium plus potassium, lowering plasma sodium despite increased sodium stores.

Plasma [Na⁺] ≈ (Naₑ + Kₑ) / TBW
Naₑ and Kₑ are exchangeable sodium and potassium; TBW is total-body water.

Learning point: Hyponatraemia does not necessarily mean sodium depletion. In the Gamblegram, the cation bar rises, but water rises proportionately further.

steps.title: Why oedema can coexist with low plasma sodium
steps.body:
Correct answer: B. Increased total-body sodium and water, with a proportionately greater increase in water.

Why it is correct: Weight gain and worsening oedema in this patient favour sodium and water retention. Low measured osmolality confirms hypotonic hyponatraemia. Water has increased disproportionately to exchangeable sodium plus potassium, lowering plasma sodium despite increased sodium stores.

Plasma [Na⁺] ≈ (Naₑ + Kₑ) / TBW
Naₑ and Kₑ are exchangeable sodium and potassium; TBW is total-body water.

Learning point: Hyponatraemia does not necessarily mean sodium depletion. In the Gamblegram, the cation bar rises, but water rises proportionately further.

steps.title: Depletion and sodium-predominant retention
steps.body:
A — Sodium and water depletion
Why it is wrong here: This pattern can cause hypovolaemic hyponatraemia, but it does not explain her weight gain and progressive oedema as well as retention. Reduced effective arterial filling in nephrotic syndrome is not the same as depleted total-body sodium.
Learning point: Assess sodium stores separately from effective circulating volume.

C — Sodium gain exceeding water gain
Why it is wrong here: With exchangeable potassium held constant in the simplified model, this would raise the cation-to-water ratio and favour hypernatraemia, whereas her plasma sodium is low.
Learning point: The direction of the sodium change depends on the relative changes in cations and water.

steps.title: Follow the oedema panel in the Gamblegram
steps.body:
D — Retention with preserved concentration
Why it is wrong here: This can produce weight gain and oedema with normal plasma sodium, as in the first stage of the Gamblegram’s oedema panel. It cannot account for her hypotonic hyponatraemia.
Learning point: Sodium retention can accompany normal, low or high plasma sodium, depending on water balance.

Take-home: Read concentration and volume separately. The animation contrasts water-predominant retention in SIADH, unreplaced water loss in DI, and sodium plus water retention in oedematous disease. Here, water gain outpaces cation gain.

steps.prompt: A 67-year-old man presents with two days of melaena and dizziness on standing. His blood pressure is 92/58 mmHg, pulse is 112/min and urine output has fallen. Urine sodium is 8 mmol/L. He is not taking diuretics. Which renal response contributes to sodium conservation in this situation?

options.text: Increased NaCl transport at the macula densa stimulates renin release.
Increased afferent arteriolar stretch stimulates renin release.
Reduced renal sympathetic beta-1 stimulation increases renin release.
Reduced NaCl transport at the macula densa stimulates renin release from juxtaglomerular granular cells.

steps.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Reduced NaCl transport at the macula densa stimulates renin release from juxtaglomerular granular cells.

Why it is correct: Blood loss, hypotension and tachycardia indicate reduced circulating volume. Reduced renal perfusion and increased upstream sodium reabsorption tend to reduce NaCl delivery and transport at the macula densa. This promotes renin release from nearby granular cells. Angiotensin II and aldosterone then support sodium retention; the low urine sodium is consistent with renal conservation.

Learning point: Use the clinical evidence of volume loss to infer the renal response. Macula-densa cells sense NaCl; juxtaglomerular granular cells release renin.

steps.title: Blood loss activates renal sodium conservation
steps.body:
Correct answer: D. Reduced NaCl transport at the macula densa stimulates renin release from juxtaglomerular granular cells.

Why it is correct: Blood loss, hypotension and tachycardia indicate reduced circulating volume. Reduced renal perfusion and increased upstream sodium reabsorption tend to reduce NaCl delivery and transport at the macula densa. This promotes renin release from nearby granular cells. Angiotensin II and aldosterone then support sodium retention; the low urine sodium is consistent with renal conservation.

Learning point: Use the clinical evidence of volume loss to infer the renal response. Macula-densa cells sense NaCl; juxtaglomerular granular cells release renin.

steps.title: Read the NaCl and pressure signals correctly
steps.body:
A — Macula-densa signal direction
Why it is wrong here: Higher macula-densa NaCl transport generally suppresses renin. Volume depletion instead tends to lower the NaCl signal, favouring renin release.
Learning point: Low macula-densa NaCl promotes renin; high NaCl tends to suppress it.

B — Afferent arteriolar stretch
Why it is wrong here: Haemorrhage reduces renal perfusion and afferent arteriolar stretch. Reduced pressure stimulates renin; increased stretch tends to suppress it.
Learning point: The renal vascular signal responds to perfusion pressure, not to plasma sodium concentration alone.

steps.title: Sympathetic input reinforces renin release
steps.body:
C — Sympathetic beta-1 signalling
Why it is wrong here: Blood loss normally increases renal sympathetic activity. Beta-1 stimulation promotes renin release; reducing that stimulation would remove a renin stimulus.
Learning point: Sympathetic beta-1 input reinforces the low-perfusion and low-NaCl signals.

Take-home: Reduced renal perfusion, reduced macula-densa NaCl transport and increased beta-1 stimulation converge on renin release. This is an appropriate response to volume loss.

steps.prompt: A 46-year-old woman is assessed for persistent hypertension and muscle weakness. Her blood pressure is 168/104 mmHg and plasma potassium is 2.8 mmol/L. She is not taking diuretics and has no vomiting or diarrhoea. Investigation shows elevated plasma aldosterone with suppressed renin. Which principal-cell change best links her hypertension and hypokalaemia?

options.text: Increased apical ENaC activity and basolateral Na+/K+-ATPase activity.
Increased apical aquaporin-2 insertion without increased sodium transport.
Inhibition of basolateral Na+/K+-ATPase, reducing cellular potassium uptake.
Reduced apical ENaC activity, making the tubular lumen less negative.

steps.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Increased apical ENaC activity and basolateral Na+/K+-ATPase activity.

Why it is correct: The findings suggest primary aldosteronism. Aldosterone increases ENaC-mediated sodium entry and supports basolateral Na+/K+-ATPase activity. Sodium retention contributes to hypertension. Electrogenic sodium reabsorption makes the lumen more negative, favouring potassium secretion through apical potassium channels and explaining hypokalaemia.

Learning point: Connect the two clinical findings to one pathway: increased distal sodium reabsorption supports volume expansion and potassium loss.

steps.title: Link hypertension and potassium loss
steps.body:
Correct answer: A. Increased apical ENaC activity and basolateral Na+/K+-ATPase activity.

Why it is correct: The findings suggest primary aldosteronism. Aldosterone increases ENaC-mediated sodium entry and supports basolateral Na+/K+-ATPase activity. Sodium retention contributes to hypertension. Electrogenic sodium reabsorption makes the lumen more negative, favouring potassium secretion through apical potassium channels and explaining hypokalaemia.

Learning point: Connect the two clinical findings to one pathway: increased distal sodium reabsorption supports volume expansion and potassium loss.

steps.title: Water channels and sodium pumps have different roles
steps.body:
B — Aquaporin-2 and water handling
Why it is wrong here: Aquaporin-2 is primarily regulated by vasopressin. Water-channel insertion alone does not explain aldosterone-driven electrogenic sodium uptake and renal potassium loss.
Learning point: Distinguish vasopressin/AQP2 water handling from aldosterone/ENaC sodium and potassium handling.

C — Basolateral pump inhibition
Why it is wrong here: Inhibiting Na+/K+-ATPase reduces the gradient for sodium entry and reduces potassium uptake into principal cells. It opposes the transport changes expected with aldosterone excess.
Learning point: The basolateral pump sustains both sodium reabsorption and the cellular potassium supply for secretion.

steps.title: ENaC activity helps determine potassium secretion
steps.body:
D — Reduced ENaC activity
Why it is wrong here: Reducing ENaC activity decreases electrogenic sodium uptake and makes the lumen less negative, reducing a driving force for potassium secretion. This is the opposite of the mechanism causing her findings.
Learning point: ENaC inhibition can promote natriuresis and spare potassium; increased ENaC activity favours potassium loss.

Take-home: High aldosterone with suppressed renin suggests renin-independent aldosterone production. Hypokalaemia is a useful clue but is absent in many patients with primary aldosteronism.

steps.prompt: A 21-year-old has recurrent visible haematuria beginning within 24 hours of upper respiratory tract symptoms. Urine contains dysmorphic red cells and protein, and serum C3 is normal. Which kidney-biopsy immunofluorescence finding would be most consistent with the suspected diagnosis?

options.text: Dominant or co-dominant mesangial IgA deposition
Strong linear IgG staining along the glomerular basement membrane
A full-house pattern with multiple immunoglobulins and complement components
Scant or absent immune deposits despite necrotising crescentic injury

steps.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Dominant or co-dominant mesangial IgA deposition

Why it is correct: Recurrent glomerular haematuria during or shortly after respiratory symptoms suggests IgA nephropathy. Its defining biopsy finding is dominant or co-dominant mesangial IgA. Normal serum C3 supports the pattern but does not establish the diagnosis; clinical suspicion and biopsy confirmation are distinct.

Learning point: Use timing to form a hypothesis and the biopsy pattern to establish the lesion.

steps.title: The timing suggests IgA nephropathy
steps.body:
Correct answer: A. Dominant or co-dominant mesangial IgA deposition

Why it is correct: Recurrent glomerular haematuria during or shortly after respiratory symptoms suggests IgA nephropathy. Its defining biopsy finding is dominant or co-dominant mesangial IgA. Normal serum C3 supports the pattern but does not establish the diagnosis; clinical suspicion and biopsy confirmation are distinct.

Learning point: Use timing to form a hypothesis and the biopsy pattern to establish the lesion.

steps.title: Linear and full-house patterns point elsewhere
steps.body:
B — Linear IgG
Why it is wrong here: Strong linear IgG along the GBM is characteristic of anti-GBM antibody disease, rather than the expected mesangial immune-deposit pattern in this case.
Learning point: Linear binding along a fixed basement-membrane antigen differs from mesangial immune-complex deposition.

C — Full-house staining
Why it is wrong here: Full-house staining includes IgG, IgA, IgM, C3 and C1q and commonly supports lupus nephritis in the right context. It is not the expected dominant mesangial IgA pattern.
Learning point: Full-house staining is a contextual clue, not a standalone diagnosis of systemic lupus.

steps.title: Pauci-immune describes deposits, not injury severity
steps.body:
D — Pauci-immune injury
Why it is wrong here: Scant immune deposits with necrotising crescentic GN are typical of an ANCA-associated pattern. IgA nephropathy is instead defined by mesangial IgA deposits.
Learning point: Pauci-immune means few immune deposits; severe inflammation and necrosis can still be present.

Take-home: Compare deposit pattern and location: mesangial IgA, linear GBM IgG, full-house immune deposits, or a pauci-immune lesion.

steps.prompt: A 10-year-old develops cola-coloured urine, periorbital oedema and hypertension about two weeks after documented streptococcal pharyngitis. Urine contains red-cell casts and serum C3 is low. Which process best explains the glomerular injury?

options.text: Direct bacterial invasion of the collecting ducts producing a suppurative infection
Autoantibody binding to type IV collagen with linear IgG deposition
ANCA-mediated neutrophil injury producing a predominantly pauci-immune lesion
Immune-mediated glomerular injury with complement activation and typically granular immune deposits

steps.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Immune-mediated glomerular injury with complement activation and typically granular immune deposits

Why it is correct: A nephritic presentation around two weeks after streptococcal pharyngitis, with low C3, supports post-streptococcal GN. Glomerular immune-mediated injury activates complement and typically produces granular immune deposits. The preceding infection triggers the immune process; it does not imply suppurative infection of the kidney.

Learning point: A latent interval after infection supports a post-infectious mechanism, in contrast to near-concurrent haematuria in typical IgA presentations.

steps.title: A delayed immune response after streptococcal infection
steps.body:
Correct answer: D. Immune-mediated glomerular injury with complement activation and typically granular immune deposits

Why it is correct: A nephritic presentation around two weeks after streptococcal pharyngitis, with low C3, supports post-streptococcal GN. Glomerular immune-mediated injury activates complement and typically produces granular immune deposits. The preceding infection triggers the immune process; it does not imply suppurative infection of the kidney.

Learning point: A latent interval after infection supports a post-infectious mechanism, in contrast to near-concurrent haematuria in typical IgA presentations.

steps.title: Infection-associated injury is not direct bacterial invasion
steps.body:
A — Direct bacterial invasion
Why it is wrong here: The case describes a delayed nephritic syndrome with red-cell casts and low C3. Direct suppurative renal infection is a different process; it does not explain the characteristic immune-mediated glomerular pattern.
Learning point: Distinguish an infection triggering GN from bacteria directly infecting urinary or renal tissue.

B — Anti-GBM antibodies
Why it is wrong here: Antibody binding to fixed type IV collagen antigens produces a linear anti-GBM pattern. The post-infectious pattern here instead favours immune-mediated injury with granular deposits.
Learning point: Linear and granular staining reflect different patterns of immune involvement.

steps.title: Complement and immune deposits help classify GN
steps.body:
C — ANCA-associated injury
Why it is wrong here: ANCA-associated GN is usually pauci-immune. The latent post-streptococcal course with low C3 is more consistent with the immune-deposit/complement pattern in answer D.
Learning point: Integrate the history, complement and biopsy pattern; low C3 alone is not specific for one GN.

Take-home: Post-streptococcal GN is one infection-related GN. Other infections and other immune diseases can also cause low complement and glomerular injury.

steps.prompt: A patient with established systemic lupus erythematosus develops proteinuria of 1.8 g/day, red-cell casts and a creatinine rise from 80 to 150 micromol/L over three weeks. C3 and C4 are low. Which approach best establishes the renal lesion and helps guide treatment?

options.text: Use the anti-double-stranded DNA titre alone to assign the histological class of lupus nephritis.
Defer renal investigation until protein excretion exceeds the nephrotic-range threshold.
Arrange prompt nephrology assessment and kidney biopsy, if feasible, to assess class, activity and chronicity.
Use renal ultrasonography to determine the glomerular immune-deposit pattern and histological class.

steps.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Arrange prompt nephrology assessment and kidney biopsy, if feasible, to assess class, activity and chronicity.

Why it is correct: Red-cell casts, substantial proteinuria and declining kidney function raise concern for active lupus nephritis. If feasible, kidney biopsy helps identify the histological class and assess active inflammation versus chronic scarring. These findings inform treatment decisions beyond what the established systemic lupus diagnosis alone provides.

Learning point: Assess the kidney lesion, not just whether the patient has systemic autoimmunity.

steps.title: Biopsy identifies the renal lesion and its activity
steps.body:
Correct answer: C. Arrange prompt nephrology assessment and kidney biopsy, if feasible, to assess class, activity and chronicity.

Why it is correct: Red-cell casts, substantial proteinuria and declining kidney function raise concern for active lupus nephritis. If feasible, kidney biopsy helps identify the histological class and assess active inflammation versus chronic scarring. These findings inform treatment decisions beyond what the established systemic lupus diagnosis alone provides.

Learning point: Assess the kidney lesion, not just whether the patient has systemic autoimmunity.

steps.title: Serology and protein quantity do not assign the class
steps.body:
A — Anti-dsDNA titre alone
Why it is wrong here: Anti-dsDNA and complement can support assessment of lupus activity, but they cannot reliably assign the renal histological class or quantify chronic scarring.
Learning point: Serology complements renal assessment; it does not replace histological classification when biopsy is indicated.

B — Waiting for nephrotic-range proteinuria
Why it is wrong here: Active lupus nephritis can occur with sub-nephrotic proteinuria. Red-cell casts and a creatinine rise already make this presentation significant.
Learning point: The nephrotic-range threshold defines a protein-excretion category, not the threshold for investigating inflammatory kidney disease.

steps.title: Ultrasound and biopsy answer different questions
steps.body:
D — Ultrasound versus microscopy
Why it is wrong here: Ultrasound assesses macroscopic anatomy, including kidney size and obstruction. It cannot resolve glomerular immune deposits or assign lupus-nephritis class.
Learning point: Light microscopy assesses structural lesions; immunofluorescence assesses immune staining; electron microscopy adds ultrastructural detail.

Take-home: Link urinary sediment and kidney-function change to prompt assessment. Biopsy class, activity and chronicity help guide care when biopsy is feasible.

steps.prompt: Over two weeks, a 56-year-old develops fatigue, nasal crusting and haemoptysis. Creatinine rises from 85 to 320 micromol/L, urine contains red-cell casts and PR3-ANCA is positive. Which kidney-biopsy pattern is most consistent with this presentation?

options.text: Crescentic glomerulonephritis with strong linear IgG along the basement membrane
Necrotising crescentic glomerulonephritis with scant or absent immune deposits
Predominantly mesangial IgA deposition without necrotising injury
A full-house pattern of granular glomerular immunoglobulin and complement deposits

steps.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Necrotising crescentic glomerulonephritis with scant or absent immune deposits

Why it is correct: Upper-airway symptoms, haemoptysis and rapidly declining kidney function with PR3-ANCA strongly suggest ANCA-associated vasculitis. The expected renal lesion is necrotising crescentic GN with scant or absent immune deposits. Possible pulmonary haemorrhage and rapid renal decline require urgent specialist assessment.

Learning point: A pauci-immune biopsy can show severe necrosis and crescent formation.

steps.title: PR3-associated disease suggests a pauci-immune lesion
steps.body:
Correct answer: B. Necrotising crescentic glomerulonephritis with scant or absent immune deposits

Why it is correct: Upper-airway symptoms, haemoptysis and rapidly declining kidney function with PR3-ANCA strongly suggest ANCA-associated vasculitis. The expected renal lesion is necrotising crescentic GN with scant or absent immune deposits. Possible pulmonary haemorrhage and rapid renal decline require urgent specialist assessment.

Learning point: A pauci-immune biopsy can show severe necrosis and crescent formation.

steps.title: A crescent is an injury pattern, not a single diagnosis
steps.body:
A — Linear GBM IgG
Why it is wrong here: Linear IgG would raise anti-GBM disease, including a possible overlapping antibody syndrome. It is not the expected pauci-immune pattern of the PR3-associated presentation.
Learning point: ANCA positivity alone does not exclude anti-GBM overlap; reconcile serology with biopsy.

C — Mesangial IgA
Why it is wrong here: Mesangial IgA supports IgA nephropathy. It is less consistent with this combined upper-airway, pulmonary and rapidly progressive PR3-associated presentation. IgA disease can itself sometimes develop crescents.
Learning point: Do not classify the cause of GN from crescents alone; deposit pattern and clinical context matter.

steps.title: Immune-deposit patterns help separate the causes
steps.body:
D — Full-house immune deposits
Why it is wrong here: A full-house pattern commonly supports lupus-associated immune-complex disease. Substantial granular immunoglobulin/complement deposits are not the expected pauci-immune pattern here.
Learning point: Immune-complex GN and pauci-immune GN can both be severe; the distinction concerns immune deposits, not simply severity.

Take-home: Crescents describe severe glomerular injury. Combine light microscopy, immunofluorescence, serology and the clinical course to identify its cause.

steps.prompt: A patient with haemoptysis and rapidly worsening kidney function has a kidney biopsy showing crescents and strong linear IgG staining along the glomerular basement membrane. Which mechanism best explains this pattern?

options.text: Autoantibodies directed against a type IV collagen antigen in the basement membrane
Mesangial deposition of IgA-containing immune complexes after mucosal immune activation
Podocyte slit-barrier dysfunction without antibody-directed basement-membrane injury
ANCA-associated neutrophil activation producing a predominantly pauci-immune lesion

steps.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Autoantibodies directed against a type IV collagen antigen in the basement membrane

Why it is correct: Strong linear IgG in a crescentic pulmonary-renal presentation supports anti-GBM disease. The classic antibody target is the non-collagenous domain of the alpha-3 chain of type IV collagen. Binding along the basement membrane explains the linear pattern. The disease requires urgent assessment.

Learning point: Connect the immune target to the staining pattern: antibody binding along a fixed GBM antigen produces linear staining.

steps.title: Linear IgG supports antibody binding to GBM antigen
steps.body:
Correct answer: A. Autoantibodies directed against a type IV collagen antigen in the basement membrane

Why it is correct: Strong linear IgG in a crescentic pulmonary-renal presentation supports anti-GBM disease. The classic antibody target is the non-collagenous domain of the alpha-3 chain of type IV collagen. Binding along the basement membrane explains the linear pattern. The disease requires urgent assessment.

Learning point: Connect the immune target to the staining pattern: antibody binding along a fixed GBM antigen produces linear staining.

steps.title: Mesangial complexes and podocyte injury are different mechanisms
steps.body:
B — IgA immune complexes
Why it is wrong here: IgA-containing immune complexes produce the characteristic mesangial deposit pattern of IgA nephropathy. They do not explain strong linear IgG along the GBM.
Learning point: The identity, location and distribution of immune deposits all contribute to the diagnosis.

C — Isolated slit-barrier dysfunction
Why it is wrong here: Podocyte slit-barrier dysfunction helps explain protein leakage, but by itself does not explain linear GBM IgG, crescentic injury and pulmonary haemorrhage.
Learning point: A structural barrier abnormality is not a substitute for identifying the immune mechanism causing the injury.

steps.title: Pulmonary-renal presentations have more than one cause
steps.body:
D — ANCA-mediated injury
Why it is wrong here: ANCA-associated vasculitis can also cause rapidly progressive GN and pulmonary haemorrhage. Its usual renal pattern is pauci-immune, whereas this biopsy has strong linear GBM IgG.
Learning point: Clinical syndromes may overlap; immunofluorescence and antibody testing help distinguish anti-GBM from ANCA-associated disease.

Take-home: Both anti-GBM disease and ANCA-associated GN may cause pulmonary-renal syndromes. The tissue immune pattern is a major discriminator; overlap can occur.

steps.title: One chain of reasoning across four weeks
steps.body:
Flow and arteriolar tone influence filtration.
A medullary gradient and vasopressin govern water recovery.
Water balance and sodium content must be distinguished.
AKI requires a search for reversible mechanisms.
Urine findings help classify glomerular disease and bleeding.
Voiding requires both contraction and outlet relaxation.
Renal tumour type, extent and patient factors guide management.

Exit prompt: choose one case and connect its mechanism to its investigation or management implication.
